newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Ex-bodyguard vows to reveal "true Yeltsin" in book.
newsitem.headline: Ex-bodyguard vows to reveal "true Yeltsin" in book.

text.p: Alexander Korzhakov, who spent a decade as Boris Yeltsin's powerful bodyguard before a bitter break-up a year ago, promised on Tuesday to reveal the Russian president in his true colours in long-awaited memoirs.

Anyone hoping for new scandals about Yeltsin at the book presentation were disappointed. Korzhakov, once touted as Russia's second most powerful man, made no new revelations just before the book goes on sale.
But he said he was ready to go to court and defend anything written in the memoirs, which he said would not please Yeltsin.
"In my book Yeltsin is a human. Not a mask, but a human," Korzhakov told a packed news conference at which he held up the sleeve of "Boris Yeltsin: From Dawn till Dusk," but not the book itself.
"Many people have written about Yeltsin... But they did not know him. What they could see was a mask. Only his family, Korzhakov's family and Yeltsin's personal friends knew him."

Korzhakov, 47, stood by Yeltsin through thick and thin as he battled the Communist Party in the late 1980s. He was at Yeltsin's side when he climbed on to a tank in 1991 to help put down a coup against then Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev.

But the two men split acrimoniously when Yeltsin fired him abruptly in June 1996 in a scandal over election campaign funding, part of a battle with Kremlin liberals who regarded his removal as vital for the president's re-election and reforms.

Korzhakov, now a member of parliament, has vowed to retaliate. Recent interviews and published extracts of the book shed light on rumours that Yeltsin enjoys a drink and allege that he tried to commit suicide more than once.
"I agree to prove everything in the court, at open sessions," said Korzhakov, wearing an open necked shirt instead of the uniform or suits he usually wore beside Yeltsin.
"I will bring there anything I want -- tapes, computer disks -- everything I have got left from my 'previous' life. This is a warning to all those who like court showcases."
He was clearly still bitter at being abandoned.
"As for returning to Boris Nikolayevich's team, no, the divorce is final and irrevocable," Korzhakov said.
He scoffed at Yeltsin's recent declarations that he has changed for the better.
"I have never heard more cynical words than his, because people, when they voted for Yeltsin, did not think that he would change that much. They voted for a different Yeltsin," he said.
"Me, too. I served a different Yeltsin. And I talk about that at length in my book."
He said he planned to add extra chapters, including revelations about Russia's disastrous war in Chechnya.
Korzhakov, who has the rank of general in the security police, did not say when the 400-page book would be issued but that he would get his copy on Wednesday.
Yeltsin's former tennis, swimming and -- some say -- drinking partner, Korzhakov was long portrayed as a shadowy and hawkish confidant whose influence went far beyond his rank.
Korzhakov accused Yeltsin, now 66, of making comments "damaging to his honour and dignity" when he was sacked, but the Supreme Court rejected his case against the president.
The Kremlin dismisses Korzhakov's remarks as those of an embittered ex-employee, not worth paying attention to.
Korzhakov said he had faced difficulties in trying to print his book and had to change publishing house because of pressure from the Kremlin.
He promised to publish his book abroad and said it could be more hard-hitting than the Russian version.
The London Sunday Times has published excerpts of the book, saying Yeltsin was ill when he failed to get off his plane to greet Irish Prime Minister Albert Reynolds during a 1994 stopover.
Korzhakov has said Yeltsin's illness may have been a stroke. He implied on Tuesday that it was brought on by alcohol.
"He was ill on the plane, but this illness was preceded by something," he told reporters.

He said Yeltsin's aides and family had probably already read the manuscript for the book but added: "As to whether they will give it to Boris Nikolayevich to read, I am 100 percent sure it won't happen."
